title: Working with Buffers
idea: Buffer methods let you create bytes from text, numbers or a size, edit them by index, and decode them with `toString(encoding)`.
points: `Buffer.from(text)` encodes text to bytes; `Buffer.from([104, 105])` takes byte values.
`Buffer.alloc(n)` makes `n` zero-filled bytes; `buf[i]` reads or writes one byte.
`toString('hex')` and `toString('base64')` write the same bytes as plain text.
`subarray` shares memory with the original; `Buffer.from(buf)` copies it.

steps.caption: `Buffer.from('cat')` encodes the text as three bytes: 99, 97, 116. `a` points at that Buffer.
`subarray(0, 2)` returns a new Buffer that is a window onto a's first two bytes. Nothing is copied.
`Buffer.from(a)` copies all three bytes into a separate Buffer. `c` has its own memory.
`b[0] = 0x62` writes through the window, so a's first byte becomes 98. The copy keeps 99.
`a` now decodes to `bat`, while the copy `c` still decodes to `cat`.

code.caption: Three routes to the same two bytes. Edit the text and watch `equals` change.

code.title: Chunks to JSON
code.caption: Data often arrives in pieces. Join the pieces first, then decode once.

pitfalls: Edits through `subarray` change the original; copy with `Buffer.from(buf)` first.
Join chunks (pieces of data) with `Buffer.concat` before decoding; a character can split across chunks.
Prefer `Buffer.alloc`; `allocUnsafe` skips zero-filling and can expose old memory.

quiz.why: `subarray` is a view on the same bytes, so writing through `b` changes `a`. `Buffer.from(a)` copied the bytes first, so `c` stays `hot`.

takeaway: `Buffer.from` makes bytes, `toString` decodes them, and `subarray` only borrows.
